Thielens Say It's High Time To Consider Hemp

By GEORGE LURIE

LIHUE -- What's all the fuss over industrial hemp? asks Peter Thielen.

It won't get you high, But ...  Peter Thielen's mother Cynthia, who happens to be a state representative from Windward Oahu's 49th district, agrees and will introduce a bill in the Legislature on Wednesday calling for state approval of privately-funded research into the viability of cultivating industrial hemp in Hawaii. This past week, Rep. Thielen also appeared before the Kauai County Council to urge members to stay out of the hemp fray -- at least for the time being.

Thielen's son Peter, admittedly, has a vested interest in getting a Hawaii hemp research project off the ground -- he is the owner of Island Hemp Wear, a local company that manufactures and wholesales a growing line of hemp clothing. See

"Hemp is not a miracle cure for our economy," Peter Thielen says. "But it would certainly solve some of our problems. Hemp can produce food, clothing, shelter, even fuel and electricity -- all from a plant grown without pesticides. Hemp could help replace some of our lost agricultural jobs and create new jobs and opportunities for the people of Kauai."

Part of the problem up to now for those pushing hemp as an ideal agricultural crop in Hawaii has been getting permission for the test project from the federal Drug Enforcement Agency, which still classifies all Cannabis sativa varieties as "marijuana" -- an illegal drug.

While it has been possible to get agency approval to grow hemp in the U.S., to date mainly for medical-marijuana uses, the DEA stipulates that any test-hemp field be secured by fence, razor wire, dogs, guards and lights -- requirements that to most potential growers are cost-prohibitive. Another big stumbling block in the effort to legalize cultivation of industrial hemp has been a lingering perception by the general public that hemp and mind-altering marijuana are one and the same.

In actuality, industrial hemp does not have enough THC content to produce even a mild high. And its cultivation would drive any nearby "pakalolo" growers away, since industrial hemp would cross-pollinate its more potent cousin, forcing it to "go to seed" and virtually killing all of its THC-producing potential. Rep. Thielen's bill, which would allow -- with DEA approval -- privately-funded hemp research in Hawaii, is one of a packet of new bills scheduled for first reading when the Legislature convenes Jan. 21.

"Once the DEA issues a research permit," says Rep. Thielen, "then this bill will make industrial hemp research test plots legal under state law."

The research test plots, Thielen says, "would be 100 percent privately funded by a publicly traded company and carried out on private agricultural land. "At this point," Thielen adds, "I'm not at liberty to say where the projectwould be and what companies are involved."

Thielen says her bill "will have good support from legislators, who recognize that industrial hemp is non-hallucinogenic and is an agricultural crop that could hold great promise for Hawaii. "I can't see any valid reason for not passing the bill," Thielen says. "There are more than 25,000 uses for this plant -- none of them drug related."

Thielen's bill notes that some 80,000 acres of agricultural land were taken out of pineapple and sugarcane production between 1984 and 1994. "There's a lot of vacant sugar land on Kauai right now," she says. "Hemp would be perfect for that land."

Her son Peter agrees. "This is a big issue for Kauai and all of Hawaii," he says. "But it's not a drug issue. This is an industrial crop, a very viable option for all of the empty sugarcane land on Kauai." Peter Thielen's Kekaha-based company, Island Hemp Wear, is two and a half years old.

"The first six months of business were the toughest," Thielen says. "We shipped maybe six dozen garments. But by the end of the first year, we were shipping $50,000 to $60,000 of goods. Last year, we saw about 600 percent growth in sales growth. This year, we're projecting business will double again." Surprisingly, Thielen says, most of his sales are on the Mainland. "We actually sell more aloha shirts in California than we do in Hawaii."

Thielen, who just turned 40, imports the hemp for his clothing from China and manufactures it on Oahu. "If the county wanted me to help bring jobs here, and if they were to offer some assistance, I'd be happy to set up the manufacturing operations right here on Kauai. "We could grow the plant here, process it into the paper or fabric we need, make up the garments here and then have a high-end product to sell nationally and internationally. We could not only provide for ourselves but also become a place where the big container ships leave with stuff rather than just drop it off.

"We are one of about four states in the nation really pressing this issue," says Peter Thielen. "Kentucky is another one. So many other industrialized nations around the world have changed their laws regarding cultivation of industrial hemp. Within two to three years, I think the U.S. will allow it as well."

Calling attention to the swiftly changing attitudes towards industrial hemp, Rep. Thielen's proposed legislation contains this language: "The State of Hawaii needs to act now to allow the planting of research plots with industrial hemp so that Hawaii -- and not its (Mainland) competitors -- will be in the position to establish important business ties with the manufacturers of hemp-based fiber, building materials, pulp, paper, oil, paints, sealants, fuel and food, and with the buyers and sellers of industrial hemp seeds."

"If the State acts now," the bill concludes, "thousands of acres of former sugarcane and pineapple lands may once again be covered in waving, vibrant masses of greenery, and this generation will have upheld its responsibility to be stewards of the land and natural resources of the State for future generations."

Council reconsiders marijuana resolution

By LESTER CHANG

LIHUE -- State House Rep. Cynthia Thielen asked the County Council Wednesday to reword its own resolution to support proposed state legislation allowing for the cultivation of industrial hemp -- long lumped with marijuana as an illegal crop -- in Hawaii. The Council's resolution essentially asked the state Legislature to leave on the books laws that make it illegal to grow marijuana -- of any kind.

But Thielen argued the measure's current wording would hinder the passage of her proposed legislation that would allow the planting of "test plots" of industrial hemp by private investors when approval by the U.S. Department of Justice is given. The Council's resolution, she added, could slow down the development of Hawaii-based industry involving industrial hemp farms and businesses that sell products using the material, she said.

"This isn't a drug issue, this is economic development," Thielen said. "It isn't a hallucinogenic drug. It is a viable economic product with 25,000 commercial uses." Research data shows that farmers could earn a profit of $190 to $500 per acre from crops of industrial hemp, she said. In Hawaii, farmers could grow two crops a year. Robert Measel Jr., who joined Thielen in asking that the Council resolution be modified, said the plants produce rich nutrients that will be put back in the soil after a harvest.

That means that any alternative crop that is planted in place of the industrial hemp will have high nutritional value, he said. And businesses that use the hemp material will have bright futures, Thielen predicted. Some U.S. companies see a future in using the hemp, even if it is illegal to grow it in the U.S. at this time, Thielen said. Interface, the largest commercial carpet company in North America, has announced it will buy and use 500,000 pounds of hemp fiber in its first year of production of hemp carpeting, Thielen said.

Interface has contracted with some Canadian farmers to buy their hemp crop to meet supply demands, Thielen said. Hemp-based carpet and diapers would be composted and would not buried at landfills. States that are looking at legalizing the cultivation of hemp plants will attract businesses that will produce hemp-based projects, she said. The Council took no action on the resolution, saying it wanted to get comments from the Kauai police and county prosecutors before it considers any changes to it. The Council will take up the matter at a meeting next Thursday.

Letter to the Editor in the same issue

Industrial hemp: a new crop

To the Forum:

A controversial resolution, addressed at the Jan. 14 County Council meeting, urges the state Legislature to keep marijuana illegal until the federal laws are changed. Testifying in opposition was state House Rep. Cynthia Thielen, who dropped everything especially to come over to Kauai, on the behest of Robert Measel Jr.

The reason for Thielen's testimony was because of a bill before the Legislature to entertain industrial hemp as an economic alternative agricultural crop.

Furthermore, she came prepared with a draft version for the County Council to utilize in drafting a resolution, which would distinguish the difference between non-hallucinogenic industrial hemp and marijuana.

Rep. Thielan presented documents containing the facts which would benefit and add to the economic stability for Hawaii. She brought finished products made of industrial hemp, such as swim trunks, aloha shirts (made by Island HEMP Wear, Kekaha), carpet samples, shoelaces and bedding fabrics, all of which are recyclable and non-polluting.

Measel also testified in opposition to the resolution, adding that Kauai could become the first island to test growing industrial hemp.

All of this testimony was sufficient factual evidence to cause Committee

Chair Ron Kouchi to defer the proposed resolution back to committee for reconsideration and further study to rewrite the resolution.

The next Council meeting is Thursday, Jan. 22, at 9 a.m. and Rep. Thielen is returning for additional testimony and support of this vital economic issue.

Deborah "Jo B"' Spence

Lihue
